steps.display: Salt on fresh okra → water pulls out
steps.narration: Sprinkle salt on fresh okra in a bowl, and soon water pools outside because thick salt draws liquid out.

steps.display: More sugar outside → water exits cell
steps.narration: When sugar water outside a plant cell is thicker than inside, water leaves through its thin skin, called osmosis.

steps.display: Vacuole shrinks → membrane pulls from wall
steps.narration: As the cell's water bag shrinks, its soft membrane pulls away from the stiff outer wall, a state called plasmolysis.

steps.display: Plasmolysis: shrinks in · Turgid: swells tight
steps.narration: Exams love swapping this with turgidity, where pure water enters the cell instead and swells it firm.

steps.display: Concentrated sugar → membrane detaches → Plasmolysis
steps.narration: Because strong sugar pulled water out here, plasmolysis fits, whereas turgidity only happens when water rushes in.

steps.display: Two brakes: backup saves · One brake: shows fault
steps.narration: With two bicycle brakes, one healthy cable covers a snapped one, while a single brake hides no faults.

steps.display: Females: X X · Males: X Y
steps.narration: In humans, females carry two matching X instruction threads, called sex chromosomes, while males carry one X and one Y.

steps.display: Faulty X hides behind healthy X
steps.narration: Haemophilia sits on the X chromosome as a weak gene, called recessive, so a healthy X hides it in women.

steps.display: Y-linked → father to every son
steps.narration: Seeing more males affected traps students into picking Y-linked, yet Y genes pass straight from fathers to sons.

steps.display: Single X in males → X-linked recessive
steps.narration: Because boys get only one X and no clotting backup on Y, X-linked recessive fits, not Y-linked dominant.

steps.display: Farm dries up → direct buyers suffer first
steps.narration: If every tomato farm dries up today, families buying straight from the farm run out of food first.

steps.display: Green plants = sunlight food makers (producers)
steps.narration: In any forest, green plants capture sunlight to make food, so they serve as the base called producers.

steps.display: Plants → Primary consumers → Higher predators
steps.narration: Plant-eaters, called primary consumers, feed straight on leaves, so losing plants cuts their meals before hunters feel it.

steps.display: Decomposers eat dead matter from all levels
steps.narration: Questions place decomposers like fungi near plants as a trap, forgetting they eat dead remains left everywhere.

steps.display: Producers gone → Primary consumers starve first
steps.narration: Caterpillars and grasshoppers eat living leaves directly, so primary consumers suffer first, while decomposers still eat dead matter.

steps.display: Soften food outside → sip dissolved broth
steps.narration: Imagine pouring warm broth onto hard food on your plate until it melts into soup, then sipping it.

steps.display: Digest outside body → absorb liquid
steps.narration: Organisms without mouths break food down outside their bodies first, a feeding method called saprophytic nutrition.

steps.display: Fungal threads → enzymes out → nutrients in
steps.narration: Fine threads push food-melting juices, called enzymes, onto dead wood or bread, then soak up the dissolved meal.

steps.display: Amoeba: swallows inside · Fungus: digests outside
steps.narration: Students often pick Amoeba by mistake, forgetting that Amoeba wraps around solid food and digests it inside.

steps.display: External enzymes + absorption → Mushroom
steps.narration: Because fungi digest food externally on dead matter and absorb liquid nutrients, mushroom fits, whereas Amoeba feeds inside.

steps.display: Ground tap: light push · Rooftop tank: strong pump
steps.narration: Filling a bucket at a low tap takes little push, while pumping water up three storeys takes heavy muscle.

steps.display: Top atria receive · Bottom ventricles pump out
steps.narration: The heart's thin upper rooms receive blood, while its lower rooms, called ventricles, grow thick muscle to pump.

steps.display: Right → nearby lungs · Left → head to toes
steps.narration: One lower room pushes gently to the nearby lungs, while the other blasts blood from head to toes.

steps.display: Right ventricle: short lung loop · Left: whole body
steps.narration: Questions make both ventricles tempting, expecting you to forget how short the trip to the lungs actually is.

steps.display: Longest body circuit → Left ventricle thickest
steps.narration: Because driving blood across the entire body needs peak force, left ventricle fits, while right ventricle serves only lungs.

steps.display: Chop outside in yard → cook inside pot
steps.narration: Just as you peel yam outside in the yard before cooking it inside a pot, cell fuel changes rooms.

steps.display: Cell jelly (stage 1) → Mitochondrion (stage 2)
steps.narration: Sugar breaks partway in the cell's watery jelly, then moves into tiny energy factories called mitochondria.

steps.display: Inner fluid of mitochondrion = matrix → Krebs cycle
steps.narration: Inside that factory's inner fluid, called the mitochondrial matrix, enzymes turn fuel around the Krebs cycle.

steps.display: Glycolysis: cytoplasm · Krebs: mitochondrial matrix
steps.narration: Because respiration begins in the cytoplasm, exams tempt you to choose cytoplasm for every later step too.

steps.display: Aerobic cycle inside powerhouse → Mitochondrial matrix
steps.narration: Since the Krebs cycle runs inside the inner powerhouse fluid, mitochondrial matrix fits, while cytoplasm holds only glycolysis.

steps.display: Wash rice: chaff drains · good grains kept
steps.narration: When you rinse rice in a sieve, dust drains out with the water while every good grain stays behind.

steps.display: Blood filtered first → useful items rescued
steps.narration: Kidneys first squeeze small substances out of blood, then sorting tubes rescue whatever the body must keep.

steps.display: All glucose reclaimed · Urea & excess leave
steps.narration: Because sugar is precious cell fuel, healthy tubes pull it all back into blood, called selective reabsorption.

steps.display: Excess mineral salts still leave in urine
steps.narration: Many students cross out mineral salts knowing we need them, forgetting our kidneys flush extra salts out daily.

steps.display: Healthy urine: no Glucose · contains excess salts
steps.narration: Because healthy kidneys reclaim all sugar, glucose is absent from urine, whereas surplus mineral salts leave regularly.

steps.display: Bright sun: draw curtains · Dusk: open wide
steps.narration: Think of window curtains at home: you pull them closer in fierce noon sun and open them wide at dusk.

steps.display: Control doorway size → protect light screen
steps.narration: Your eye protects its back screen the same way by shrinking or widening the dark opening in front.

steps.display: Iris muscles adjust pupil: small in sun, wide in dark
steps.narration: That coloured muscular ring is the iris: its muscles pull the doorway narrow in sun and open in dim rooms.

steps.display: Iris: brightness amount · Lens: sharp focus
steps.narration: Exams trap students into picking the lens, mixing up controlling how bright light is with focusing a sharp picture.

steps.display: Regulates light amount entering eye → Iris
steps.narration: Changing how much light enters belongs to the iris, whereas the lens only bends light to sharpen focus.

steps.display: Helper 1 → student · Helper 2 → packed food
steps.narration: Picture two helpers arriving at boarding school: one becomes the student, while the other packs the chop-box.

steps.display: Pollen tube delivers 2 male cells into ovule
steps.narration: In flowering plants, a pollen tube carries two male cells into one seed chamber, triggering double fertilisation.

steps.display: 1 + 1 = diploid zygote · 1 + 2 = triploid endosperm
steps.narration: One joins the egg into a two-set zygote, while the second joins two helpers into three-set endosperm food.

steps.display: Two fusions ≠ two twin embryos
steps.narration: Hearing double fertilisation fools students into picturing twin embryos, yet each ovule holds just one egg.

steps.display: Diploid zygote + triploid endosperm nucleus
steps.narration: One fusion builds the baby and one builds food, making diploid zygote and triploid endosperm right, not twin embryos.

steps.display: Two unrelated towns → same river paddle shape
steps.narration: Picture strangers in two distant river towns carving identical flat paddles simply because water pushes every boat the same.

steps.display: Different ancestors + same habitat → similar tools
steps.narration: When unrelated animal groups share one environment, their bodies grow matching tools, a pattern called convergent evolution.

steps.display: Whales (mammals) + Fish → flat swimming paddles
steps.narration: Whales evolved from land mammals while fish began in seas, yet water shaped both into streamlined swimmers.

steps.display: Convergent: grow alike · Divergent: split apart
steps.narration: Exams test the opposite term, divergent evolution, where related cousins branch away from one limb plan.

steps.display: Unrelated whale + fish flippers → Convergent evolution
steps.narration: Because mammals and fish came from separate branches and grew alike to swim, convergent evolution fits, not divergent.
